items.title: Why the genocide verdict against Myanmar has big implications for Israel | Geoffrey Robertson
items.summary:
Proving the ‘crime of crimes’ against an individual is notoriously difficult, but the ICJ has set a precedent for states to be found liable. Israel could be next

For the first time ever, a state has been found guilty of genocide – that “crime of crimes” – and has been ordered to compensate victims and to prosecute and punish the perpetrators. This judgment came from the international court of justice (ICJ), which has convicted Myanmar of killing and expelling many thousands of Rohingyas in Rakhine state in 2017.

The court did not change “as such” the definition of the crime, settled by the genocide convention in 1948 as requiring proof of an intention to destroy, in whole or part, a racial or religious group. But it made the prospect of proving this against a nation a good deal easier than against an individual. It set a precedent for its next case concerning state liability, namely the case brought by South Africa against Israel.

Geoffrey Robertson KC was a UN appeal judge and is author of World of War Crimes – Eyeless in Gaza and Beyond

Continue reading...
items.t: Why the genocide verdict against Myanmar has big implications for Israel | Geoffrey Robertson

items.title: Is Trump Ever To Blame? Should You Trust Him Or Our Enemies?
items.summary:
(Photo by Win McNamee/Getty Images) 

The FAA imposed an aviation ground stop across the entire country a couple of weeks ago, leaving tens of thousands of travelers stranded.

Naturally, the president, as all good leaders do, accepted responsibility.

Ha! Just kidding.

President Donald Trump’s precise words were, “I don’t accept any responsibility.”

What a guy! 

Many of us remember when the country was assigning responsibility for a shortage of COVID tests on the day Trump declared the coronavirus outbreak to be a national emergency. In the words of our noble leader: “I don’t take responsibility at all.”

Of course not.

This got me to thinking: Is Trump consistent about this?

Happily, John Dickerson recently provided the answer, giving examples of the many times Trump has declined responsibility for anything that went wrong in America. Dickerson’s list includes:

In February 2017, after Navy SEAL Ryan Owens died in the first raid (in Yemen) of Trump’s presidency. Trump pointed to the generals who had brought him the plan: “And they lost Ryan.” 

Yes, they did, sir! Responsibility lies with the generals, not the commander-in-chief!

In January 2019, having told Democratic leaders he would “take the mantle” for a government shutdown, Trump paraphrased Harry Truman once the shutdown dragged on: “The buck stops with everybody.” 

On April 27, 2020, when asked whether he bore any responsibility for a spike in poison-hotline calls after he mused about injecting disinfectant: “No, I don’t.”

items.title: The GC’s Superpower Is Changing Altitude
items.summary:
A dashboard says customer commitments are being reviewed on time. An employee keeps a private spreadsheet because the approved system cannot handle a recurring exception.

Both can be true in the same hypothetical company.

The dashboard captures completion. The spreadsheet captures the work required to make completion possible. A GC looking at only one of them has a partial account of the process.

That is why the most useful part of the Shibuya Crossing metaphor is the ability to move between viewpoints. The person above the crossing can see routes. The person walking through it knows which route is blocked, which sign is confusing, and where someone needs more time.

For a general counsel, changing altitude means connecting those forms of knowledge.

At the matter level, you need the particular promise, technical fact, and consequence. At the workflow level, you can examine repeated handoffs and workarounds. At the enterprise level, you can ask which incentives, authorities, and assumptions are producing the pattern.

Each level should inform the others. An executive interpretation that cannot survive contact with an actual matter needs revision.

Research on organizational networks offers a useful connection. In “Structural Holes and Good Ideas,” Ronald Burt examines the value of bridging separated groups. That research supports interest in access to different perspectives. It does not establish that a GC’s title automatically supplies such access.

I would treat the enterprise perspective as something a legal leader must keep earning.

items.t: The GC’s Superpower Is Changing Altitude

items.title: Orrick Matches Cravath On Raises And Bonuses, Translated From Orrick-Speak
items.summary:
Orrick has made its compensation move, and it’s unsurprisingly a full market match, following the standard Cravath finally set last week . That means the $235,000-to-$455,000 salary scale Milbank introduced back in June, plus Cravath’s year-end bonuses, plus Cravath’s newly beefed-up special bonuses.

At least, that’s what it says once you translate it. Orrick doesn’t do class years, so instead of the same chart everyone else uses, they have titles like Associate, Managing Associate, and Senior Associate, each with their own levels. It makes the org chart look a bit more like a Dungeons & Dragons character sheet, but we can basically translate “Level 2 Managing Associate” as a fifth-year.

The memo, from the firm’s talent leadership, opens the way these always open:

Thank you for all your hard work and your commitment to our standards of excellence. It is contributing to an incredibly successful year — in terms of our market impact, client relationships and opportunities to collaborate across our firm.

“Opportunities to collaborate across our firm” is a such a pleasant phrasing for getting staffed on a deal at 11 p.m.

Special bonuses run from $11,000 to $40,000, an exact match for Cravath’s specials , which came in over Milbank’s summer specials of $6,000 to $25,000. Merit bonuses run from $20,000 up to the familiar $115,000. Max it out and the most senior associates take home $155,000 in bonuses, same as at Cravath. Counsel get the top $40,000 special and the $115,000 merit bonus too.

Orrick’s come with this:

Special bonuses will be paid December 31, 2026, to all who…

items.title: The Trump DOJ Pushed Out Its Best Lawyers, Now They Want Jobs Investigating It
items.summary:
For nearly two years, the Trump Justice Department has handled its career lawyers like a disposable resource: fire the ones who worked on the wrong cases, drive out the rest, and backfill with true believers who answer the “forward this to a friend” email. Now a lot of those lawyers are sending their résumés somewhere new… the committee that’s about to investigate the Justice Department.

According to MS NOW, roughly 500 people have applied for investigative and oversight jobs on the House Judiciary Committee, which Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-MD) is set to chair when Democrats take control of the House in January. Per two people familiar with the applications, many of the people hoping to help Raskin probe the Trump DOJ are current or former employees of that same department.

Welp, that tracks.

The DOJ has shed 21 percent of its attorneys , more than 2,600 lawyers, and plenty of them didn’t leave voluntarily. The department fired the prosecutors who worked for Jack Smith, and then went after the ones who enforced federal abortion clinic protections . When it noticed nobody was left to do the work, it dropped the requirement that prosecutors have any legal experience at all , offered $25,000 signing bonuses , and watched its once-prestigious Honors Program struggle to find takers .

A spokesperson for House Judiciary Democrats told MS NOW it’s not a huge surprise that DOJ alums and staff are lining up, and was pretty direct about why:

Which is a bold play with a judge who’s already bent over backwards for your client!

items.title: Sam Alito Jokes About AI Brain Upload Staying On Supreme Court Forever
items.summary:
Lord Alito of Trenton has informed the realm that he will not be abdicating. 

The Supreme Court justice — who already added a knighthood to his monarchical resume — just collected the Irving Kristol Award at the American Enterprise Institute’s annual gala. The award celebrates an individual who has made “intellectual or practical contributions to public policy, social welfare, or political understanding.” Failing that, they gave it to the guy who threw a temper tantrum at the State of the Union and benefited from his own draft opinion totally coincidentally getting leaked right as his colleagues prepared to water it down. 

Graced with this honor, Justice Samuel Alito took the opportunity to speak about himself — specifically about how he plans to work his way into the record books by climbing the Supreme Court’s longevity rankings :

If I can hang on for five more years, I will reach 26th place. Ten years, 15th place. And in 16 years, if AI has not killed off humanity, I will have passed every former justice.

That would place Alito around 92 years old, clinging to one of the most powerful jobs in public service for the sake of his own vanity. Note how lawyerly “every former justice” is. Clarence Thomas, who is very much a current justice, passes William O. Douglas’s record on May 20, 2028. If Thomas managed to make it until he’s 92, Alito would have to hold on until he’s 105.

Though Alito has an answer for that too:

JUSTICE ALITO on eventually being the longest serving justice — "in 16 years, if AI has not killed off humanity, I will have passed every former justice."…
items.t: Sam Alito Jokes About AI Brain Upload Staying On Supreme Court Forever

items.title: Biglaw Firm Moves Associates To The ‘Cravath Scale’ — If They Hit Their Hours
items.summary:
K&L Gates has made its 2027 compensation move. In an email to U.S. associates, Global Managing Partner Stacy Gray Ackermann and the firm’s Management Committee announced that associates who hit their hours will move to “the Cravath scale” next year. That runs from $235,000 for first-years up to $455,000 for eighth-years. The firm is also publishing its associate bonus scale for the first time.

Good news for K&L Gates associates. Weird name for it, though.

The scale K&L Gates is adopting was created by Milbank, which announced the raises back in June with an effective date of July 1, 2026. Cravath didn’t make its move until last week, with salaries effective January 1, 2027. Calling it the Cravath scale anyway just goes to show how ingrained Cravath’s role as comp leader is, even when they aren’t the ones doing the leading. It’s the same cascade we’ve watched for years : Milbank starts it, Cravath blesses it, and only then does the rest of Biglaw feel safe falling in line.

Above the Law, for its part, will give Milbank its flowers, calling it the Milbank scale, named for the firm that gave associates the raises a full six months before the rest of these followers.

Now for K&L’s fine print, because there’s a lot of it. The new salaries aren’t automatic. Associates need at least 1,950 creditable hours, including at least 1,850 billable, and they have to be in “good standing.” That means meeting the firm’s performance expectations on work quality, judgment, responsiveness, reliability, and professionalism, and complying with its time submission policy. items.title: Elite Litigation Boutique Pays Bonuses Up To $187.5K
items.summary:
Biglaw is just getting its bonus season underway. At Reid Collins & Tsai, they’re already on round four of bonuses.

When we checked in with the elite litigation boutique in August, its third round brought associate bonuses to $130,000 to $170,000 for the year at that point. What does compensation look like at the firm right now? 

Base pay for Reid Collins associates runs from $225,000 (junior associate) to $275,000 (senior associate 1) to $325,000 (senior associate 2). On top of those salaries, associates will receive fourth quarter bonuses, bringing total annual bonus amounts to $150,000 to $187,500.

For a little perspective, Milbank raised market salaries to $235,000 to $455,000 in June and followed up with $6,000 to $25,000 in special bonuses in July . Cravath matched the raises for its listed classes effective January 1 and upped the specials to $11,000 to $40,000 . Its year-end scale held steady at $15,000 to $115,000, with both bonuses prorated for the newest class. That’s up to $155,000 combined at Cravath. Reid Collins topped that by $32,500.

Senior founding partner Bill Reid says this is the first year the firm has paid bonuses in all four quarters to every lawyer and staff member. The 40-lawyer firm had a record year, and Reid says nine-figure annual revenue is looking like the norm.

Bill Reid, the firm’s senior founding partner, told Above the Law:

Our philosophy is simple. It takes the whole team to win a case, so when we get a result for a client, we pay bonuses to the entire team then and there. Why wait until year-end?

items.title: The Second Amendment and an "unusually dangerous" approach to dicta
items.summary:
Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff. 

***

On November 10, The New York Times published an article suggesting that a major piece of the Supreme Court’s Second Amendment jurisprudence is premised on a misquote by the late Justice Antonin Scalia in his 2008 majority opinion in D.C v. Heller , in which the court held that there was an individual right to possess firearms. The essence of the piece is that Scalia used the phrase “dangerous and unusual” to describe those weapons not protected by the right to keep and bear arms, attributing this terminology primarily (or perhaps solely) to the 18th century British jurist William Blackstone. Yet Blackstone’s writings instead use the phrase “dangerous or unusual.”

According to the Times piece, “[t]he consequences of Justice Scalia’s use of ‘and’ rather than ‘or’ have been profound”: “Since all guns are dangerous, courts have had to focus instead on determining whether a type of firearm is unusual, often parsing marketing data and consumer surveys to gauge a weapon’s popularity.” Presumably, if Scalia had used the phrase “dangerous or unusual,” it would be easier for legislatures to ban even certain commonly owned firearms because dangerousness alone would be sufficient to bring a category of weapons outside the amendment’s protective sphere.

The Times story has reverberated quickly, with strong backlash from conservative lawyers and scholars. Such disagreements have focused largely on the specific citation Scalia used.…
items.t: The Second Amendment and an "unusually dangerous" approach to dicta

items.title: Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson and the arc of the law
items.summary:
In September, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson received an award named after the late Justice William Brennan, a liberal lion. In her acceptance speech, Jackson discussed Brennan’s role as the Supreme Court became more conservative, noting that he “believed that even his dissents could make a difference and remind the nation that the pursuit of equal justice under law is an ongoing effort.” Jackson indicated that she agreed with that idea, telling the audience that she saw “dissent[s] as more than just a disagreement with the outcome of a case, I see them as an expression of faith in the future and a demonstration of hope.” As she put it, “However desolate the moment feels, we who write for a future age have hope that the noble and collective work of bending the long arc of the law toward justice will continue.”

Since joining the court in the summer of 2022, Jackson has sought to promote her understanding of that view. Although she has been consistently part of the court’s liberal bloc, even among the three Democratic appointees she has forged a unique role. As her invocation of Brennan suggests, it often appears that her goal is not simply to express disagreement with the majority, but to offer an alternative vision and to speak to the public directly – even if she does so without the support of her fellow liberals.
items.t: Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson and the arc of the law

items.title: The Supreme Court and profanity
items.summary:
Around 2 p.m. on October 30, 1973, John Douglas was driving with his 15-year-old son when he heard a litany of profanity come over the radio. New York’s WBAI, a nonprofit radio station, was airing a program on modern attitudes toward language. Near the end, the station played George Carlin’s “ Filthy Words ” routine, which begins with the comedian saying he’d been thinking about “the words you couldn’t say on the public airwaves; the ones you definitely wouldn’t say, ever.” He went on to repeat those words several times, contrasting them with words like “bastards,” “hell,” and “damn,” which were mostly acceptable, and showing how even some of his list of seven were perfectly fine in other contexts. His point was to show the absurdity of profanity.

The station later said it had chosen Carlin’s routine because it was an “incisive satirical view of the subject under discussion,” in the style of other great satirists like Mark Twain or Mort Sahl. Carlin, the station explained, was doing more than “mouthing obscenities.” He was “using words to satirize as harmless and essentially silly our attitudes towards those words.” 

Before playing the routine, the host had warned that it included language some listeners might find offensive and suggested they return in 15 minutes if they were inclined toward offense. But about a month later, John Douglas complained to the Federal Communications Commission about the transmission which he said was “garbage” and had been broadcast in the presence of his “young son.” He was the only listener to do so. A member of Morality in Media who…
items.t: The Supreme Court and profanity

The international court of justice has settled questions over the issue of intent, with powerful implications for Israel

The international court of justice (ICJ) decision last Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya recognizes the plight of one of the world’s most persecuted minorities. It also resonates in Gaza, where the same court is now more likely to find that Israel committed genocide against Palestinians.

items.title: AI Use Guidelines: It’s Complicated. It’s Also Not A Choice
items.summary:
The other day, I gave a presentation to a group of lawyers and legal professionals about AI use and its benefits and risks. As is my practice, I stressed the need for law firms of any and all sizes to have strong AI-use guidelines. I stressed that these guidelines should cover things like which tools are approved for use, the need to protect confidentiality, and the need to verify all citations and other information from any AI output. 

And of course, I also talked about the risks of not having an AI use policy. The risk of unauthorized or shadow use of unapproved tools, the risk of confidentiality breaches, and the risk of citations to hallucinated cases and propositions. My standard shtick.

But for some reason, it occurred to me right before this presentation that I should also mention an added reason for robust AI use guidelines. And that is that good guidelines could protect a law firm if someone goes rogue and fails to verify citations before filing them in a court document. I usually don’t talk much about this since it seems rather obvious. But as it turns out, I was prescient to do so. 

On November 13, 2026, the Delaware Court of Chancery issued an order sanctioning a lawyer who signed a brief with hallucinated citations. But it exonerated his law firm because it had proper AI use guidelines in place. 

The Wrong Way 

Here’s what happened. A lawyer submitted fabricated quotations and mischaracterized legal authorities in a brief. After he was outed by the other side, he owned up to it. Sort of. He filed a “corrected” brief. That brief removed quotation marks…

items.title: Some Law Firm Names Are Simply Too Long
items.summary:
Lawyers understandably have a certain amount of pride when it comes to seeing their names on the doors of law firms. Indeed, many lawyers work their entire careers with the hope that they will one day become a named partner of a law firm and have their name adorn letterhead, business cards, and other materials associated with a law practice. Moreover, adding a lawyer’s name a law firm can be an effective way to recognize that attorney’s contributions to a practice without necessarily altering the financial arrangements among the partners. However, some law firm names are simply too long. Law firms should generally have no more than four names for a variety of practical reasons.

Earlier in my career, I worked at a law firm that had four names. Although the name of the firm was somewhat lengthy, it was not particularly difficult to recite the name of the firm when answering the phone or introducing myself to other lawyers. At some point during my tenure at this law firm, the firm added a fifth name.

For whatever reason, adding that fifth name made it exponentially more difficult to say the name of the law firm. One would think that adding another name would only make it marginally more cumbersome to recite the name of the firm. However, there seems to be a point at which a law firm’s name becomes too much of a mouthful, and in my experience, the distinction between four and five names can be surprisingly significant.

This can be especially annoying for lawyers who need to identify themselves and their law firms numerous times throughout the day. When appearing in court,…
items.t: Some Law Firm Names Are Simply Too Long

items.title: DOJ Demand To Hide Misconduct Inside Special Master Fails To Impress Judge

Woodward’s entire job consists of parachuting in to courtrooms where the government is in trouble and making matters so much worse . In Chicago, US Attorney Andrew Boutros’s office was already flailing after being forced to dismiss charges against the “Broadview 6” for obstruction of a government official in the conduct of his duties, i.e., getting hit by an ICE agent’s car in the middle of a protest. The government spent months indignantly denouncing the allegations of prosecutorial misconduct as “fevered paranoia and delusional speculation.” But the unsealed grand jury transcripts showed three separate presentations to the same panel in October of 2025, each of which was plagued by obvious impropriety.

In open court, USA Boutros assured Judge Perry that he only discovered the problem five months later. And his office assured the court that they’d had no discussions with Main Justice about the case.

items.title: Criminal law is constitutional law
items.summary:
With arguments over the Second Amendment and the Excessive Fines Clause on the near horizon, this column seeks to provide some tranquil and more generalized ideas – a moment of Thanksgiving holiday respite. Whether you are a Supreme Court follower who usually shunts criminal law to the side, or an experienced criminal law reader who might enjoy some holiday dinner thoughts for your friends and family, this column seeks to demonstrate that much of criminal law is actually constitutional law – and perhaps show why that can be so interesting. To do so, I will scatter some examples from last term, drawn from my recently published Annual Review of the Supreme Court’s Term, Criminal Cases booklet. When explaining criminal law to your friends or just opining over Thanksgiving dinner, I’d like to show why your mantra should be “crim law is con law” and vice versa .

Winship – criminal law fundamentals are constitutional law 

Every criminal law class I have taught over 40 years, from 1L first semester through advanced criminal procedure or federal criminal law, has begun with the same case: 1970’s In re Winship . Even non-lawyers know from film and TV that the prosecution’s high burden for proof in a criminal case is beyond a reasonable doubt. But do they know that this is constitutionally required? And perhaps more interesting, that this standard is nowhere, textually, in that document?

items.t: Criminal law is constitutional law

items.title: Even justices have regrets
items.summary:
In June 2023, the court decided Students for Fair Admissions, Inc. v. University of North Carolina , holding that race-conscious admissions at Harvard and the University of North Carolina violated the Constitution. Chief Justice John Roberts’ majority opinion in the case, along with Justice Brett Kavanaugh’s concurrence , cited Justice Sandra Day O’Connor’s 2003 prediction in Grutter v. Bollinger that “25 years from now, the use of racial preferences will no longer be necessary to further” student body diversity.

But the justices did not account for one thing, according to Brooklyn Law School Professor Yuvraj Joshi : O’Connor’s later misgivings about that statement. In interviews with her biographer after she left the court, O’Connor acknowledged that the 25-year figure “may have been a misjudgment.” When asked for a new estimate, she replied, “[t]here’s no timetable. You just don’t know.”
items.t: Even justices have regrets

items.title: Calls for court packing fail the test of history
items.summary:
Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff.

As Democrats have taken control in Congress, we can expect calls for court packing to intensify. One especially prominent proposal has been to expand the court to 13 justices. In the last few months, we have seen former Vice President Kamala Harris say the Supreme Court should be increased to this number. In August, Rep. James Clyburn, a longtime Democratic leader in the House, endorsed this proposal on “Meet the Press.” Just in the past few weeks, Hillary Clinton said the party “should seriously look at expanding the court while the Democrats are in power.” Potential presidential candidate Pete Buttigieg has advocated increasing the number of justices to 13 as well.

Some of these calls come with superficially plausible justifications. Take Hillary Clinton’s proposal, for instance. “It used to be that you’d have one justice for each circuit,” Clinton explained. “We now have 13 circuits, we should have 13 justices.” Buttigieg has also argued for modifying the size of the court on that basis. But the symmetry argument is pretextual: It is no mere coincidence that the reintroduction of a one-to-one justice to circuit relationship under Democratic control would produce exactly the four seats needed to transform the current six-to-three conservative majority into a seven-to-six liberal one. Such a proposal then allows advocates to cover their desire for change to the court’s size in the language of a seemingly neutral…

items.title: Five major issues that may still make it onto this term’s oral argument docket
items.summary:
Time is running out for the justices to add cases to this term’s oral argument docket . Under the Supreme Court’s typical briefing schedule , a case must be granted by mid-January to be briefed in time for the final argument session, which begins this term on April 19.

But despite being short on time, the justices are not short on major petitions for review . Over the next two months, they will likely consider petitions addressing such high-profile issues as the Trump administration’s ban on transgender servicemembers, state laws requiring Ten Commandments displays in public school classrooms, and the regulation of prediction markets like Kalshi.

Understanding the timeline 

Before we explore some of the major issues pending before the Supreme Court, let me first offer a brief refresher on how a petition for review makes it to the oral argument docket. (For more on this process, read law professor Stephen Wermiel’s SCOTUSblog column from last week.)

Litigants file a petition for review, also known as a petition for certiorari, at the Supreme Court when they want the justices to review a lower court ruling against them. In their petition, they lay out, among other things, their views on why the ruling was wrong and why the issue is worthy of the justices’ attention.

After a petition is filed, the litigants that prevailed before the lower court (known as the respondents) have 30 days to respond, although they may ask for additional time. Sometimes, they file a brief in which they agree that the Supreme Court should take up the issue, but it’s far more common for…
items.t: Five major issues that may still make it onto this term’s oral argument docket
